proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(\ell\), and put
\[
p^0_{\ell t}=\Pr\{Y_{t_\ell}(0)>y_0\mid G=g_\ell\}.
\]
By no anticipation, the treated-group pre-period untreated exceedance probability is \(r_{\ell1}\).  The normal-link parallel-trends equality therefore gives
\[
 q(p^0_{\ell t})-q(r_{\ell1})=q(r_{\ell2})-q(r_{\ell3}),
\]
and hence, because \(\Phi\) and \(q=\Phi^{-1}\) are mutually inverse on \((0,1)\),
\[
p^0_{\ell t}
=\Phi\{q(r_{\ell1})+q(r_{\ell2})-q(r_{\ell3})\}
=H(r_{\ell1},r_{\ell2},r_{\ell3}).
\]
The treated-post exceedance probability is \(r_{\ell4}\).  Taking complements at the fixed threshold and subtracting therefore yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta_\ell
&=\Pr\{Y_{t_\ell}(1)\le y_0\mid G=g_\ell\}
 -\Pr\{Y_{t_\ell}(0)\le y_0\mid G=g_\ell\}\\
&=(1-r_{\ell4})-(1-p^0_{\ell t})
=H(r_{\ell1},r_{\ell2},r_{\ell3})-r_{\ell4}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is an equality between the causal target and a functional of the four observed marginal laws; it is not a definition of the causal target.  Averaging this equality over the fixed \(L\) pairs identifies \(\overline\Delta=L^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^L\Delta_\ell\).  Finally, the outcome-independent split only selects which observations estimate each already-defined marginal \(r_{\ell j}\); it changes neither the displayed population probabilities nor the identification equality.

Fix \(\ell\) and suppress its index.  Set \(b=\rho c_3\), \(x=\log(c_1/c_3)\), \(z=\log(c_2/c_3)\), and
\[
R_b(x,z)=\log\Phi\{q(be^x)+q(be^z)-q(b)\}-\log b-x-z.
\]
The coefficient and rarity assumptions imply that every probability appearing here or on the line segments below belongs to \((0,1)\).  Since \(q'(p)=1/\phi(q(p))\) and \(p=\Phi(q(p))\),
\[
\frac{d}{da}q(be^a)=\frac{be^a}{\phi(q(be^a))}
=\frac{1}{m(q(be^a))}.
\]
Writing \(S=q(be^x)+q(be^z)-q(b)\), two ordinary differentiations give
\[
\partial_{xz}R_b(x,z)
=\frac{m'(S)}{m(q(be^x))m(q(be^z))}.
\]
Moreover \(R_b(x,0)=R_b(0,z)=0\) exactly.  The two-dimensional fundamental theorem of calculus on the signed rectangle from \((0,0)\) to \((x,z)\) consequently gives
\[
R_b(x,z)=xz\int_0^1\!\int_0^1
 \frac{m'\{q(be^{sx})+q(be^{tz})-q(b)\}}
 {m(q(be^{sx}))m(q(be^{tz}))}\,dt\,ds
=A B_\rho.
\]
This formula remains valid when either side of the signed rectangle is zero; no division by \(x\), \(z\), or \(A=xz\) has occurred.

Direct differentiation of \(m=\phi/\Phi\) yields
\[
m'(v)=-m(v)\{v+m(v)\}.
\]
For \(v\ge0\), the bracket is positive.  For \(v=-a<0\), \(a>0\),
\[
\Phi(-a)=\phi(a)\int_0^\infty e^{-at-t^2/2}\,dt
<\phi(a)\int_0^\infty e^{-at}\,dt=\frac{\phi(a)}a,
\]
so \(m(-a)>a\), and the bracket is again positive.  Thus \(m'(v)<0\) for every real \(v\).  All denominator factors in the integral are positive, whence \(B_\rho<0\).

By common rarity, \(be^x=\rho c_1\), \(be^z=\rho c_2\), and \(be^{x+z}=\rho Q\).  Exponentiating the identity for \(R_b\) gives
\[
H(r_1,r_2,r_3)=\rho Q e^{AB}.
\]
Therefore, using \(e^w-1=w\psi(w)\),
\[
\Delta-\Delta^P
=H(r_1,r_2,r_3)-\rho Q
=\rho Q A B\psi(AB)
=\rho Q A C_\rho.
\]
The integral definition of \(\psi\) shows \(\psi(w)>0\) for every real \(w\); hence \(C_\rho=B\psi(AB)<0\).  Since \(\rho Q>0\) and \(C_\rho\ne0\), equality \(\Delta=\Delta^P\) is equivalent to \(A=xz=0\), which is equivalent to \(c_1=c_3\) or \(c_2=c_3\).

Fix a pair \(\ell\), suppress its index, and write \(a_n=(\rho_n/n)^{1/2}\).  The add-half estimator satisfies the exact decomposition
\[
\widetilde r_j-r_j
=\frac{K_j-n_jr_j}{n_j+1}+\frac{1/2-r_j}{n_j+1}.
\tag{1}
\]
The second term is \(O(n^{-1})=o(a_n)\), because \(n\rho_n\to\infty\) and the role shares are bounded below.  For fixed real \(t_1,\ldots,t_4\), expansion of the logarithm of the characteristic function of the independent centered Bernoulli sums in (1) gives
\[
\log\mathbb E\exp\left\{i\sum_{j=1}^4t_j\sqrt{\frac n{\rho_n}}
\frac{K_j-n_jr_j}{n_j+1}\right\}
=-\frac12\sum_{j=1}^4t_j^2\frac{c_j}{\pi_j}+o(1).
\]
Indeed, the quadratic term is the displayed limit, while the sum of absolute third-order terms is bounded by a constant times \((n\rho_n)^{-1/2}\); the maximal normalized summand has the same order.  Thus
\[
\sqrt{\frac n{\rho_n}}(\widetilde r-r)
\ \Rightarrow\ N\!\left(0,\operatorname{diag}\left(\frac{c_1}{\pi_1},\ldots,\frac{c_4}{\pi_4}\right)\right).
\tag{2}
\]
The same calculation for the fixed sixty cells and mutual independence gives joint convergence with independent pair coordinates.

For \(P(p)=p_1p_2/p_3-p_4\),
\[
\nabla P(r)=\left(\frac{c_2}{c_3},\frac{c_1}{c_3},-\frac{c_1c_2}{c_3^2},-1\right).
\tag{3}
\]
On the event \(\max_j|\widetilde r_j/r_j-1|\le1/2\), whose probability tends to one by (1) and \(n\rho_n\to\infty\), the Hessian of \(P\) is \(O(\rho_n^{-1})\).  Hence its Taylor remainder is
\[
O_P\!\left(\rho_n^{-1}\|\widetilde r-r\|^2\right)=O_P(n^{-1})=o_P(a_n).
\]
Combining (2)--(3) gives
\[
\frac{\widehat\Delta^P-\Delta^P}{\sqrt{\rho_nV/n}}\Rightarrow N(0,1),
\tag{4}
\]
because the variance obtained from (2)--(3) is
\[
\frac{c_4}{\pi_4}
+\frac{Q^2}{\pi_1c_1}+\frac{Q^2}{\pi_2c_2}+\frac{Q^2}{\pi_3c_3}=V>0.
\]

We next treat the exact map directly, rather than differentiating an asymptotic error formula.  If \(s=q(p_1)+q(p_2)-q(p_3)\) and \(e=(1,1,-1)\), then
\[
H_j(p)=e_j\frac{\phi(s)}{\phi(q(p_j))},
\]
and
\[
H_{jk}(p)=H_j(p)\left\{-\frac{s e_k}{\phi(q(p_k))}
+\mathbf1\{j=k\}\frac{q(p_j)}{\phi(q(p_j))}\right\}.
\tag{5}
\]
Repeating the quantile-shift and Mills-remainder estimates from the common-cutoff proof on the fixed compact coefficient interval \([1/4,6]\) (their derivation uses only positivity and finite compact endpoints) gives, uniformly on the preceding high-probability neighborhood,
\[
H(r)=\rho_nQ\{1+O(u_n^{-2})\},\qquad
\frac{m(s)}{m(q(r_j))}=1+O(u_n^{-2}).
\]
Since \(\phi(v)=\Phi(v)m(v)\), (5) consequently gives
\[
\nabla\{H(p_1,p_2,p_3)-p_4\}\big|_{p=r}
=\nabla P(r)+O(u_n^{-2}).
\tag{6}
\]
Also (5), \(|s|+|q(r_j)|=O(u_n)\), and \(\phi(q(r_j))=r_jm(q(r_j))\asymp\rho_nu_n\) show that the exact-map Hessian is \(O(\rho_n^{-1})\) on the same high-probability neighborhood.  Its Taylor remainder is therefore again \(o_P(a_n)\).  Equations (2), (5), and (6) prove
\[
\frac{\widehat\Delta^E-\Delta}{\sqrt{\rho_nV/n}}\Rightarrow N(0,1).
\tag{7}
\]

The exact factorization and the uniform coefficient theorem give, without an additive error that could dominate near a cancellation plane,
\[
\frac{\Delta^P-\Delta}{\sqrt{\rho_nV/n}}
=\frac{Q}{\sqrt V}\frac{A\sqrt{n\rho_n}}{u_n^2}
\{1+O(u_n^{-2})\}
=\frac{Q}{\sqrt V}\Lambda_n\{1+O(u_n^{-2})\}.
\tag{8}
\]
Thus, if \(\Lambda_n\to\lambda\), adding (8) to (4) gives the asserted noncentral normal limit.  The coefficient limits imply \(Q_n/\sqrt{V_n}\to Q/\sqrt V\in(0,\infty)\).  Subtracting the Taylor expansions behind (4) and (7) also gives
\[
\frac{\widehat\Delta^P-\widehat\Delta^E}{\sqrt{\rho_nV/n}}
=\frac{Q}{\sqrt V}\Lambda_n\{1+o(1)\}+o_P(1).
\]
Consequently the two estimators differ by \(o_P(\sqrt{\rho_n/n})\) if and only if \(\Lambda_n\to0\).  Repeating the argument over the fixed set of \(L\) pairs proves the stated joint limits and independence.

Let
\[
\overline{\widehat\Delta}^{,P}=L^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^L\widehat\Delta^P_\ell,
\qquad
\overline{\widehat\Delta}^{,E}=L^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^L\widehat\Delta^E_\ell,
\qquad
\overline\Delta^{,P}=L^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^L\Delta^P_\ell.
\]
The centered Taylor and characteristic-function argument in the pairwise proof does not require convergence of the drifting cancellation indices.  It gives, jointly over the fixed pairs,
\[
\frac{\widehat\Delta^P_\ell-\Delta^P_\ell}{\sqrt{\rho_n/n}}
\Rightarrow N(0,V_\ell),
\qquad
\frac{\widehat\Delta^E_\ell-\Delta_\ell}{\sqrt{\rho_n/n}}
\Rightarrow N(0,V_\ell),
\]
with independent coordinates.  Since
\(
\overline V=L^{-2}\sum_{\ell=1}^LV_\ell>0,
\)
finite-dimensional characteristic functions therefore give
\[
\frac{\overline{\widehat\Delta}^{,P}-\overline\Delta^{,P}}
{\sqrt{\rho_n\overline V/n}}\Rightarrow N(0,1),
\qquad
\frac{\overline{\widehat\Delta}^{,E}-\overline\Delta}
{\sqrt{\rho_n\overline V/n}}\Rightarrow N(0,1).
\tag{1}
\]
By the definition of \(b_n\), the exact deterministic centering difference is
\[
\frac{\overline\Delta^{,P}-\overline\Delta}
{\sqrt{\rho_n\overline V/n}}
=\frac{\sqrt{n/\rho_n}}{L\sqrt{\overline V}}
\sum_{\ell=1}^L(\Delta^P_\ell-\Delta_\ell)=b_n.
\tag{2}
\]
Adding (2) to the first convergence in (1) proves the \(N(b,1)\) limit whenever \(b_n\to b\).  The second convergence in (1) proves the centered exact-link limit.

The gradient comparison in the pairwise proof is uniform over the finite set of pairs, so summing its Taylor expansions yields
\[
\frac{\overline{\widehat\Delta}^{,P}-\overline{\widehat\Delta}^{,E}}
{\sqrt{\rho_n\overline V/n}}=b_n+o_P(1).
\tag{3}
\]
Thus aggregate first-order equivalence is equivalent to \(b_n\to0\), not to coordinatewise vanishing of all pairwise shifts.

For completeness, the distinction is nonvacuous.  Take two pairs with \((c_1,c_2,c_3)=(2,2,1)\) and \((1/2,4,1)\), respectively, and put all remaining pairs on a cancellation plane.  The two nonzero leading signed coefficients satisfy
\[
Q_1A_1=4(\log2)^2,
\qquad Q_2A_2=-4(\log2)^2.
\]
Along a sequence with \(\sqrt{\tau_n}=u_n^3\), the uniform expansion makes their summed population shift \(O(\rho_nu_n^{-4})\), and hence \(b_n=O(u_n^{-1})\to0\), whereas each individual standardized leading shift has magnitude of order \(u_n\).  Integer \(n\) may be chosen along a subsequence with \(n\rho_n/u_n^6\to1\).  This exhibits aggregate cancellation while neither individual shift vanishes.

For each fixed cell, the probability generating function is
\[
\mathbb E s^{K_{\ell j,n}}
=\{1+r_{\ell j,n}(s-1)\}^{n_{\ell j}}.
\]
The common-rarity, coefficient-limit, and role-share assumptions imply
\[
n_{\ell j}r_{\ell j,n}\to\pi_{\ell j}\tau c_{\ell j},
\qquad n_{\ell j}r_{\ell j,n}^2\to0.
\]
Taking logarithms of the generating function therefore gives the limit
\(
\pi_{\ell j}\tau c_{\ell j}(s-1).
\)
Mutual independence and the fixed number of cells yield the joint product-Poisson limit \(K\Rightarrow Z\).

Define
\[
a_{\ell j,n}=n\widetilde r_{\ell j}
=\frac{n(K_{\ell j,n}+1/2)}{n_{\ell j}+1}.
\]
The count-vector convergence and positive share limits give jointly
\[
a_{\ell j,n}\Rightarrow W_{\ell j}=\frac{Z_{\ell j}+1/2}{\pi_{\ell j}}.
\]
Every \(W_{\ell3}\) is strictly positive.  Hence ordinary algebra on the finite-dimensional vector gives
\[
n\widehat\Delta^P_\ell
=\frac{a_{\ell1,n}a_{\ell2,n}}{a_{\ell3,n}}-a_{\ell4,n}
\Rightarrow T_\ell.
\tag{1}
\]

To compare the exact map, first restrict to the event \(\max_{\ell,j}K_{\ell j,n}\le M\).  On that event all \(a_{\ell j,n}\) lie, for large \(n\), in a compact subinterval of \((0,\infty)\) depending only on \(M\) and the role-share bounds.  The common-cutoff proof applies verbatim to any such fixed compact coefficient interval, with \(1/n\) as its rarity scale.  Its factorization gives uniformly on the event
\[
nH(a_{\ell1,n}/n,a_{\ell2,n}/n,a_{\ell3,n}/n)
=\frac{a_{\ell1,n}a_{\ell2,n}}{a_{\ell3,n}}+O(u_n^{-2}),
\tag{2}
\]
where now \(u_n=-q(1/n)\to\infty\).  The limiting Poisson vector is tight, so the probability of the complement can be made arbitrarily small by first choosing \(M\) and then taking \(n\) large.  Removing the cutoff in (2) proves
\[
n\widehat\Delta^E_\ell-n\widehat\Delta^P_\ell\to_P0.
\]
Together with (1), this proves the two statistic limits jointly.

For the population target, exact factorization and the uniform coefficient result give
\[
H(r_{\ell1},r_{\ell2},r_{\ell3})
=\rho_nQ_{\ell n}\{1+O(u_n^{-2})\}.
\]
Because \(n\rho_n\to\tau<\infty\), coefficient convergence yields
\[
n\Delta_{\ell n}
=n\rho_n(Q_{\ell n}-c_{\ell4,n})+o(1)
\longrightarrow\tau(Q_\ell-c_{\ell4}).
\]
Averaging (1)--(2) over fixed \(L\) gives the asserted aggregate limit.  If \(\tau=0\), every limiting Poisson variable is zero, so
\[
W_{\ell j}=\frac1{2\pi_{\ell j}},
\qquad
T_\ell=\frac{\pi_{\ell3}}{2\pi_{\ell1}\pi_{\ell2}}
-\frac1{2\pi_{\ell4}}.
\]
Its average is the displayed deterministic limit and can be nonzero when the four shares differ.

The set \(\mathcal P_0\) is an intersection of closed linear half-spaces and a box, hence is compact and convex.  If \(p\in\mathcal P_0\) has a zero coordinate, the inequalities \(p_i\le8p_j\) force every coordinate to be zero.  Thus every nonzero point is strictly positive.

At a positive point put \(t=\max(p_1,p_2,p_3)\), \(v=-q(t)\), and write
\[
q(p_i)=-v-d_i,qquad i=1,2,3.
\]
Since \(\phi(w)\le\phi(0)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}<1/2\),
\[
\Phi(-1/2)=\frac12-\int_0^{1/2}\phi(w)\,dw>\frac14.
\]
Because \(t\le1/4\), one therefore has \(v>1/2\).  Comparable rarity gives \(t/8\le p_i\le t\), and the identity
\[
\log\frac{t}{p_i}=\int_v^{v+d_i}m(-w)\,dw
\]
together with \(m(-w)>w\) gives
\[
0\le d_i\le d:=\frac{\log8}{v}.
\tag{1}
\]
Let \(s=q(p_1)+q(p_2)-q(p_3)\).  The elementary bounds following from (1) are
\[
|s-q(p_i)|\le2d,
\qquad |s+q(p_i)|\le2v+3d.
\]
Since \(\log8<3\) and \(v^{-2}<4\),
\[
\left|\frac{s^2-q(p_i)^2}{2}\right|
\le2\log8+\frac{3(\log8)^2}{v^2}<114.
\tag{2}
\]
At positive points,
\[
\left|\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i}\right|
=\frac{\phi(s)}{\phi(q(p_i))}
=\exp\left\{\frac{q(p_i)^2-s^2}{2}\right\}<e^{114}<2^{256}.
\]
The last numerical inequality follows from \(\log2>1/2\).  Since the derivative of \(-p_4\) is \(-1\), (2) gives
\[
\|\nabla G(p)\|_1<3\cdot2^{256}+1<2^{258}=L_{\rm lip}
\tag{3}
\]
throughout the positive part of the cone.

We also verify the boundary value needed to integrate (3).  Along any positive sequence tending to the origin, set \(\rho=t/4\) and \(c_i=p_i/\rho\) for \(i=1,2,3\).  Then \(c_i\in[1/2,4]\) and \(\rho\downarrow0\).  The inverse-tail integral identity
\[
\frac{\Phi(-v)}{\phi(v)}=\frac1v\int_0^\infty e^{-a}e^{-a^2/(2v^2)}\,da
\]
and (1) show that the combined normal index equals \(-v+e_v\), where \(|e_v|\le3\log(8)/v\).  Moreover, for \(w\ge1\), restricting the integral to \([0,1]\) gives
\[
\frac{\Phi(-w)}{\phi(w)}\ge
\frac1w\int_0^1e^{-a-a^2/2}\,da=\frac{c_0}{w},
\qquad c_0:=\int_0^1e^{-a-a^2/2}\,da>0,
\]
and hence \(m(-w)\le w/c_0\).  If \(e_v\le0\), monotonicity gives \(\Phi(-v+e_v)\le\Phi(-v)\).  If \(e_v>0\), then for all sufficiently large \(v\),
\[
\log\frac{\Phi(-v+e_v)}{\Phi(-v)}
=\int_{v-e_v}^{v}m(-w)\,dw
\le \frac{ve_v}{c_0}\le\frac{3\log8}{c_0}.
\]
Thus \(H(p_1,p_2,p_3)=O\{\Phi(-v)\}=O(t)=O(\rho)\).  The cone inequalities also give \(p_4=O(t)\), so \(G(p)\to0=G(0)\).  Thus \(G\) is continuous at the only boundary point where differentiability was not asserted.

For positive \(p,p'\), the line segment joining them stays in the positive part of the convex cone, so integration of (3) gives
\[
|G(p)-G(p')|\le L_{\rm lip}\|p-p'\|_\infty.
\]
If one endpoint is the origin, apply this inequality to an interior point of the segment and pass to the origin using the proved continuity.  This establishes the global certificate.

Fix one pair, write \(n_j\) for its four role sizes, \(M_n=\sum_jn_j\), and let \(x_j=k_j/n_j\).  Define the polynomial likelihood without combinatorial factors by
\[
L_k(p)=\prod_{j=1}^4p_j^{k_j}(1-p_j)^{n_j-k_j},
\qquad
L_{\rm sat}=L_k(x)>0,
\]
with \(0^0=1\).  The endpoint conventions in the Bernoulli divergence give the exact extended-real identity
\[
D_p(k)=2\{\log L_{\rm sat}-\log L_k(p)\}.
\tag{1}
\]
Put \(t=L_{\rm sat}e^{-4/\beta}\).  Certified rational upper and lower exponential series bounds produce, after finitely many terms, a positive rational \(t_{\rm lo}\) satisfying
\[
t/2\le t_{\rm lo}\le t.
\tag{2}
\]
Choose a positive rational mesh \(h\) with
\[
M_nh\le t_{\rm lo}/4,
\qquad L_{\rm lip}h\le\eta/8,
\tag{3}
\]
and partition \([0,1/4]^4\) into finitely many rational boxes of max-diameter at most \(h\).

For each box \(B\), feasibility of \(B\cap\mathcal P_0\) is decidable using rational arithmetic: enumerate quadruples of active rational boundary hyperplanes, solve every nonsingular rational system, and check its solution against all inequalities.  A nonempty bounded rational polytope has a vertex, and at a vertex the active normals span \(\mathbb R^4\), so this finite enumeration also returns a rational feasible point \(p_B\).  For one coordinate, the absolute derivative of \(p^k(1-p)^{n-k}\) is at most \(n\) on \([0,1]\).  Telescoping over four coordinates therefore gives
\[
|L_k(p)-L_k(p')|\le M_n\|p-p'\|_\infty.
\tag{4}
\]
Thus \(U_B=L_k(p_B)+M_nh\) is a rational upper enclosure on \(B\).  Retain exactly the feasible boxes with \(U_B\ge t_{\rm lo}\).

At a positive rational feasible point, \(G(p_B)\) has a certified rational enclosure of any prescribed positive width.  One completely finite construction is to enumerate rational lower and upper brackets for each inverse normal quantile and certify strict CDF inequalities by rational Taylor bounds for the exponential integral; a bracket of the requested width exists by continuity and strict monotonicity.  Enumerating pairs, rather than bisecting at a possibly exact equality, guarantees termination.  Applying the same certified CDF enclosure to the resulting normal-index interval gives a rational interval \([a_B,b_B]\ni G(p_B)\) of width at most \(\eta/4\).  At \(p_B=0\), use the exact enclosure \([0,0]\).  The global Lipschitz lemma implies
\[
G(B\cap\mathcal P_0)\subset
[a_B-L_{\rm lip}h,b_B+L_{\rm lip}h].
\tag{5}
\]
Take the rational hull of these intervals and round outward on a rational grid of width at most \(\eta/2\); if there is no retained box, return \([0,0]\).  Every enumeration, series refinement, and grid is finite, proving termination and rationality.

If \(p\in\mathcal R_\beta(k)\), then (1) gives \(L_k(p)\ge t\ge t_{\rm lo}\).  Its feasible box satisfies \(U_B\ge L_k(p)\), is retained, and (5) contains \(G(p)\).  Hence the returned interval contains \(G(\mathcal R_\beta(k))\).  An empty retained list therefore implies \(\mathcal R_\beta(k)=\varnothing\).

For coverage, first take positive \(p\in\mathcal P_0\).  The elementary inequality \(\log y\le y-1\) gives
\[
\operatorname{KL}\{\operatorname{Bern}(x),\operatorname{Bern}(p)\}
\le\frac{(x-p)^2}{p(1-p)}.
\]
Therefore, under the four independent binomial marginals,
\[
\mathbb E_pD_p(K)
\le2\sum_{j=1}^4n_j
\frac{\mathbb E_p(K_j/n_j-p_j)^2}{p_j(1-p_j)}=8.
\]
Markov's inequality yields
\[
\Pr_p\{p\notin\mathcal R_\beta(K)\}
=\Pr_p\{D_p(K)>8/\beta\}\le\beta.
\tag{6}
\]
At the origin, \(K=0\) almost surely, the origin's box obeys \(U_B\ge L_k(0)=L_{\rm sat}=1\), and so it is retained.  Thus (6) and the image containment prove the uniform \(1-\beta\) coverage, including the origin.

It remains to prove the expected-diameter order.  If \(B\) is retained, (3)--(4) imply
\[
L_k(p_B)\ge t_{\rm lo}-M_nh\ge3t_{\rm lo}/4.
\]
Every feasible point in that box has likelihood at least \(t_{\rm lo}/2\ge t/4\), and hence, by (1), belongs to
\[
\mathcal R'(k)=\{p\in\mathcal P_0:D_p(k)\le q'\},
\qquad q'=8/\beta+2\log4.
\tag{7}
\]
For Bernoulli laws, Jensen's inequality applied to \(-\log\), followed by \(-\log a\ge1-a\), gives
\[
\operatorname{KL}\{\operatorname{Bern}(x),\operatorname{Bern}(p)\}
\ge(\sqrt x-\sqrt p)^2+(\sqrt{1-x}-\sqrt{1-p})^2.
\]
Consequently every \(p\in\mathcal R'(k)\) satisfies
\[
|\sqrt{p_j}-\sqrt{x_j}|\le d_j:=\sqrt{\frac{q'}{2n_j}}.
\tag{8}
\]
For any two such points, (8) gives
\[
|p_j-p'_j|\le4\sqrt{x_j}d_j+4d_j^2.
\tag{9}
\]
The Lipschitz image bound, (5), and the final outward rounding show that the output diameter is at most a fixed multiple of
\[
L_{\rm lip}\sum_{j=1}^4\{\sqrt{x_j/n_j}+1/n_j\}+\eta.
\]
Since \(\mathbb E_p\sqrt{x_j}\le\sqrt{p_j}\), \(p_j=\rho c_j\le4\rho\), and \(n_j\ge\underline\pi n\), taking expectations proves
\[
\sup_{p=\rho c}\mathbb E_p\operatorname{diam}\mathsf{Outer}_{\beta,\eta}(K)
\le C_\beta\left\{\sqrt{\frac\rho n}+\frac1n+\eta\right\}
\le C_\beta\left\{\frac{\max(1,\sqrt{n\rho})}{n}+\eta\right\}.
\]
Here \(C_\beta<\infty\) depends only on \(\beta\), the fixed share bounds, and the fixed certified Lipschitz constant.

For \(k=0\), the origin argument above proves retention.  If instead \(k_j=n_j\) for every \(j\), then \(L_{\rm sat}=1\) and every feasible \(p\) satisfies \(L_k(p)\le4^{-\sum_jn_j}\).  A retained feasible point would, by (2)--(4), satisfy \(L_k(p_B)\ge t/4\), which is impossible when
\[
2\sum_{j=1}^4n_j\log4>8/\beta+2\log4.
\]
Thus the retained list is empty under the stated all-full condition and the algorithm returns exactly \([0,0]\).

The identification proposition gives \(\Delta_\ell=G(r_{\ell1},\ldots,r_{\ell4})\).  Because \(r_{\ell j}=\rho c_{\ell j}\), the coefficient and rarity bounds imply \(r_\ell\in\mathcal P_0\).  When \(\eta\le1/n\), the rational outer-interval theorem, applied pairwise with \(\beta=\alpha/L\), gives
\[
\Pr(\Delta_\ell\notin I_\ell)\le\frac{\alpha}{L}.
\]
When \(\eta>1/n\), the same conclusion follows directly from equations (1)--(6) of that theorem's proof: the construction and coverage argument use only \(\eta>0\), and its diameter proof gives the same bound with the now larger additive term \(\eta\).  Thus the marginal guarantee and diameter order hold for every positive rational \(\eta\).
No cross-pair independence is needed for the union bound, which yields
\[
\Pr\{\Delta_\ell\in I_\ell\text{ for every }\ell\}
\ge1-\sum_{\ell=1}^L\frac\alpha L=1-\alpha.
\]
On this simultaneous event, if \(I_\ell=[L_\ell,U_\ell]\), then
\[
L^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^LL_\ell
\le L^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^L\Delta_\ell
\le L^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^LU_\ell,
\]
so \(\overline\Delta\in\overline I\).  Finally,
\[
\operatorname{diam}(\overline I)
=L^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^L\operatorname{diam}(I_\ell).
\]
Taking expectations and applying the pairwise diameter bound with the fixed value \(\beta=\alpha/L\) proves the asserted order after absorbing the fixed number \(L=15\) into \(C_\alpha\).

Fix \(\ell\) and write \(p_j=p^\circ_{\ell j}\).  The interior margin places \(p=(p_1,\ldots,p_4)\) in a compact subset of \((0,1)^4\), on which the exact-link map
\[
g(p)=H(p_1,p_2,p_3)-p_4
\]
is twice continuously differentiable with bounded Hessian.  With
\(
v=q(p_1)+q(p_2)-q(p_3),
\)
direct differentiation gives
\[
\nabla g(p)=\left(
\frac{\phi(v)}{\phi(q(p_1))},
\frac{\phi(v)}{\phi(q(p_2))},
-\frac{\phi(v)}{\phi(q(p_3))},
-1\right)=\gamma^\circ_\ell.
\tag{1}
\]
The add-half identity
\[
\widetilde r_j-p_j
=\frac{K_j-n_jp_j}{n_j+1}+\frac{1/2-p_j}{n_j+1}
\tag{2}
\]
shows that the deterministic smoothing term is \(O(n^{-1})=o(n^{-1/2})\).  Taylor expansion of \(g\), using the bounded Hessian and \(\widetilde r-p=O_P(n^{-1/2})\), then gives
\[
\sqrt n\{\widehat\Delta^E_\ell-\Delta_\ell\}
=\sum_{j=1}^4\gamma^\circ_{\ell j}
\frac{\sqrt n}{n_{\ell j}+1}
\sum_{a=1}^{n_{\ell j}}(E_{\ell ja,n}-p^\circ_{\ell j})+o_P(1).
\]
Because \(n_{\ell j}/n\to\pi_{\ell j}>0\), replacing \(\sqrt n/(n_{\ell j}+1)\) by \(1/(\sqrt n\,\pi_{\ell j})\) changes the expression by \(o_P(1)\).  This proves the asserted linear representation with
\[
\iota^\circ_{\ell j}(e)=\frac{\gamma^\circ_{\ell j}}{\pi_{\ell j}}
(e-p^\circ_{\ell j}).
\]
For clarity, the characteristic function of the resulting centered sum has logarithm
\[
-\frac{t^2}{2}\sum_{j=1}^4
\frac{(\gamma^\circ_{\ell j})^2p^\circ_{\ell j}(1-p^\circ_{\ell j})}{\pi_{\ell j}}+o(1),
\]
because its maximal summand is \(O(n^{-1/2})\).  It therefore converges to \(N(0,\Omega^\circ_\ell)\).  Mutual independence of all role observations gives independent limits across the fixed pairs.  Averaging the linear representations yields
\[
\sqrt n\left\{L^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^L\widehat\Delta^E_\ell-\overline\Delta\right\}
\Rightarrow N\!\left(0,L^{-2}\sum_{\ell=1}^L\Omega^\circ_\ell\right).
\]
Finally, the identification proof shows that splitting does not change the population DTT functional.  The displayed interior margin, positive limiting shares, and gradient (1) are precisely the fixed-threshold standard-normal specializations named in the benchmark assumptions; the treated-post derivative is the additional \(-1\) component.  Thus the mathematical limit is the stated split-role specialization and does not assert a boundary extension of the published interior theorem.

theorem.statement:
There are universal finite constants \(M>0\) and \(\rho_0\in(0,1/16]\) such that, simultaneously for every \(1\le\ell\le L\), every \(0<\rho\le\rho_0\), and every \((c_{\ell1},c_{\ell2},c_{\ell3})\in[1/2,4]^3\),
\[
\left|u^2 C_{\rho,\ell}+1\right|\le \frac{M}{u^2}.
\]
The same bound holds on both exact cancellation planes \(x_\ell=0\) and \(z_\ell=0\).  Equivalently, uniformly on the complete coefficient box, \(C_{\rho,\ell}=-u^{-2}+O(u^{-4})\) as \(\rho\downarrow0\), without any division by \(A_\ell\).
theorem.proof_tex:
We give a common-cutoff proof and keep all estimates uniform in the coefficient box.  For \(v>0\), the substitution \(w=v+s/v\) gives the exact identity
\[
\frac{\Phi(-v)}{\phi(v)}
=\frac1v\int_0^\infty e^{-s}e^{-s^2/(2v^2)}\,ds.
\]
Taylor's theorem at a nonnegative argument gives
\[
e^{-a}=1-a+\frac{a^2}{2}+r(a),\qquad |r(a)|\le\frac{a^3}{6}.
\]
Since \(\int_0^\infty e^{-s}s^k\,ds=k!\), integration produces
\[
\frac{\Phi(-v)}{\phi(v)}
=\frac1v\left(1-v^{-2}+3v^{-4}+\varepsilon_v\right),
\qquad |\varepsilon_v|\le15v^{-6}.
\tag{1}
\]
For \(v\ge2\), the bracket in (1) is bounded away from zero.  Multiplication of finite polynomials, followed by the identity
\[
\frac1{1+h}=1-h+h^2-\frac{h^3}{1+h},
\]
applied to \(h=-v^{-2}+3v^{-4}+\varepsilon_v\), shows that there is an absolute \(K_0<\infty\) such that
\[
\left|m(-v)-\left(v+v^{-1}-2v^{-3}\right)\right|\le K_0v^{-5}.
\tag{2}
\]
The exact identity \(m'(-v)=-m(-v)\{m(-v)-v\}\), rather than differentiation of a remainder, then implies for another absolute \(K_1\)
\[
\left|m'(-v)-\left(-1+v^{-2}\right)\right|\le K_1v^{-4}.
\tag{3}
\]

It remains to put every quantile in (2)--(3) under one cutoff.  Let \(u=-q(\rho)\), and for \(|a|\le\log4\) put \(v_a=-q(\rho e^a)\).  Choose \(u_0\) so large that
\[
e^{3u_0^2/8}>4,
\qquad u_0\ge4.
\]
Because \(m(-w)>w\),
\[
\log\frac{\Phi(-u/2)}{\Phi(-u)}
=\int_{u/2}^{u}m(-w)\,dw
>\frac{3u^2}{8}.
\]
Thus, whenever \(u\ge u_0\), all probabilities between \(\rho/2\) and \(4\rho\) have inverse-tail magnitudes at least \(u/2\).  Also
\[
\frac{d}{da}v_a=-\frac1{m(-v_a)},
\]
and integration along the interval joining \(0\) and \(a\) yields
\[
|v_a-u|\le\frac{2\log4}{u}.
\tag{4}
\]
Every geometric interpolation \(c_3^{1-s}c_1^s\) and \(c_3^{1-t}c_2^t\) remains in \([1/2,4]\).  Hence (4) applies to the two denominator quantiles in the definition of \(B_{\rho,\ell}\).  It also shows that the negative of the combined numerator argument
\[
q(\rho c_3^{1-s}c_1^s)+q(\rho c_3^{1-t}c_2^t)-q(\rho c_3)
\]
equals \(u+O(u^{-1})\), uniformly in \(s,t\in[0,1]\), the pair index, and all three coefficients.  Increasing \(u_0\), if necessary, makes all these magnitudes at least \(2\).

Substitution into (2)--(3) now gives constants \(K_2,K_3<\infty\), independent of all indices and coefficients, for which
\[
m\{q(\rho c_3^{1-s}c_1^s)\}=u+O(u^{-1}),\qquad
m\{q(\rho c_3^{1-t}c_2^t)\}=u+O(u^{-1}),
\]
and
\[
\frac{m'\{q(\rho c_3^{1-s}c_1^s)+q(\rho c_3^{1-t}c_2^t)-q(\rho c_3)\}}
{m\{q(\rho c_3^{1-s}c_1^s)\}m\{q(\rho c_3^{1-t}c_2^t)\}}
=-u^{-2}+E_{s,t},qquad |E_{s,t}|\le K_3u^{-4}.
\tag{5}
\]
Integrating (5) over the unit square proves
\[
B_{\rho,\ell}=-u^{-2}+O(u^{-4})
\tag{6}
\]
uniformly on the entire coefficient box.  In particular, this step did not divide by \(x_\ell z_\ell\).

Finally, \(|A_\ell|\le(\log8)^2\), so (6) gives \(|A_\ell B_{\rho,\ell}|=O(u^{-2})\).  From the integral representation of \(\psi\),
\[
|\psi(w)-1|
\le \int_0^1 t|w|e^{|w|}\,dt
\le\tfrac12|w|e^{|w|}.
\]
Consequently \(\psi(A_\ell B_{\rho,\ell})=1+O(u^{-2})\), and
\[
C_{\rho,\ell}=B_{\rho,\ell}\psi(A_\ell B_{\rho,\ell})
=-u^{-2}+O(u^{-4})
\]
with one common constant.  Choose \(\rho_0=\min\{1/16,\Phi(-u_0)\}\) and enlarge the finite constant to \(M\).  When \(x_\ell=0\) or \(z_\ell=0\), the definition gives \(A_\ell=0\) and \(\psi(A_\ell B_{\rho,\ell})=1\), while (5)--(6) are unchanged.  This proves the claimed certificate on both planes.

proposed_statement_changes.proposed:
Suppose \(\alpha\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1)\), set \(\beta=\alpha/L\), and let \(\eta>0\) be the predeclared rational tolerance.  Then
\[
\Pr\{\Delta_\ell\in I_\ell\text{ for every }1\le\ell\le L\}\ge1-\alpha
\quad\text{and}\quad
\Pr\{\overline\Delta\in\overline I\}\ge1-\alpha.
\]
There exists a finite constant \(C_\alpha\), depending only on \(\alpha\) and the fixed role-share bounds, such that
\[
\mathbb E\{\operatorname{diam}(\overline I)\}
\le C_\alpha\left\{\frac{\max(1,\sqrt{n\rho})}{n}+\eta\right\}.
\]
proposed_statement_changes.reason: The current claim invokes a finite rational algorithm at \(\beta=\alpha/L\), but \(\alpha\) is presently an arbitrary real and therefore \(\beta\) need not be a rational algorithmic input. For an arbitrary noncomputable real \(\alpha\), finite rational termination is not defined. The proposed claim adds only rationality of \(\alpha\); the proof shows directly that the displayed coverage and diameter conclusions hold for every positive rational tolerance \(\eta\), including \(\eta>1/n\).

proposed.statement:
For rational \(\beta\in(0,1)\) and \(0<\eta\le1/n\), \(\mathsf{Outer}_{\beta,\eta}\) terminates after finitely many rational operations and certified normal-CDF enclosures, returns a rational interval containing \(G(\mathcal R_{\beta}(K))\), and satisfies
\[
\inf_{p\in\mathcal P_0}\Pr_p\{G(p)\in\mathsf{Outer}_{\beta,\eta}(K)\}\ge1-\beta.
\]
There exists a finite constant \(C_{\beta}\), depending only on the fixed role-share bounds, such that
\[
\sup_{p=\rho c}\mathbb E_p[\operatorname{diam}\mathsf{Outer}_{\beta,\eta}(K)]
\le C_{\beta}\{\max(1,\sqrt{n\rho})/n+\eta\}.
\]
The all-zero table retains the origin.  The all-full table produces an empty retained list whenever \(2\sum_{j=1}^{4}n_j\log4>8/\beta+2\log4\).
proposed.justification: The theorem gives boundary-valid coverage on every count table together with a finite certificate and a rare-regime length guarantee.
proposed.gap: Sachs, Gabriel, and Fay provide valid continuum inversion and a stochastic approximation, not a deterministic outer certificate with this diameter order.
proposed.consumer: Small-block distributional-DiD studies can report intervals that remain defined at zero counts and can be independently audited.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The proof of finite-sample coverage uses \(K_j\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n_j,p_j)\) and hence \(\operatorname{Var}(K_j/n_j)=p_j(1-p_j)/n_j\). Marginal Bernoulli sampling alone does not imply this variance identity. The already-frozen mutual-independence assumption supplies exactly the missing premise; this edit changes only the dependency metadata, not the claim.

proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(M>0\). By the definition of \(\Phi\), its density \(\phi\) is strictly positive, so for \(a<b\),
\[
\Phi(b)-\Phi(a)=\int_a^b\phi(w)\,dw>0.
\]
Thus \(\Phi\) is strictly increasing. Moreover, \(\Phi(-M)>0\), because it is the integral of the strictly positive function \(\phi\) over the nonempty interval \(( -\infty,-M]\).

By \(\rho_n\to0\), for this fixed \(M\) there is an integer \(n_M\) such that
\[
4\rho_n<\Phi(-M)\qquad(n\ge n_M).
\]
The common-rarity equality and the upper endpoint of the coefficient box give, simultaneously for every \(1\le\ell\le L\) and \(j\in J\),
\[
0<r_{\ell j,n}=\rho_n c_{\ell j,n}\le4\rho_n<\Phi(-M),
\qquad n\ge n_M.
\]
Here positivity follows from \(\rho_n>0\) and \(c_{\ell j,n}\ge1/2\), while \(r_{\ell j,n}<1\) is part of the declared probability-array type, so \(q(r_{\ell j,n})\) is well defined. Since \(q=\Phi^{-1}\) and \(\Phi\) is strictly increasing, the preceding display implies
\[
q(r_{\ell j,n})<-M.
\]
Consequently, using the defining formula for the standard-normal density,
\[
0<\phi(q(r_{\ell j,n}))
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
  \exp\!\left\{-\frac{q(r_{\ell j,n})^2}{2}\right\}
\le \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-M^2/2}.
\]
Because \(L=15\) and \(J=\{1,2,3,4\}\) are finite, taking the maximum preserves this bound:
\[
0\le
\max_{1\le\ell\le L,\,j\in J}\phi(q(r_{\ell j,n}))
\le \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-M^2/2},
\qquad n\ge n_M.
\]
For every \(\varepsilon>0\), one can choose \(M>0\) so that \((2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-M^2/2}<\varepsilon\). The preceding display then proves
\[
\max_{1\le\ell\le L,\,j\in J}\phi(q(r_{\ell j,n}))\longrightarrow0.
\]

Finally, suppose for contradiction that a constant \(C\) with \(0<C<\infty\) satisfied
\[
\inf_{\ell,j,n}\phi(q(r_{\ell j,n}))\ge \frac1C.
\]
The positivity and finiteness of \(C\) ensure that \(1/C>0\). For every \(n\), the alleged bound would imply
\[
\max_{1\le\ell\le L,\,j\in J}\phi(q(r_{\ell j,n}))\ge\frac1C,
\]
contradicting the just-proved convergence to zero. Therefore no finite positive uniform inverse-density constant exists. Since the cited Assumption 5 is precisely the requirement of such a positive uniform lower bound, it excludes every array in the comparable-rarity sequence, even though each finite-\(n\) cell probability remains strictly positive.

proposed_statement_changes.proposed: For the standard-normal link, every comparable-rarity triangular array satisfying \(r_{\ell j,n}=\rho_n c_{\ell j,n}\), \(c_{\ell j,n}\in[1/2,4]\), and \(\rho_n\to0\) obeys \(\max_{1\le\ell\le L,\,j\in J}\phi(q(r_{\ell j,n}))\to0\). Hence no constant \(C\) with \(0<C<\infty\) can make \(\inf_{\ell,j,n}\phi(q(r_{\ell j,n}))\ge1/C\), so Djuazon and Tsyawo's Assumption 5 excludes the entire comparable-rarity sequence rather than merely failing at an exact zero cell.
proposed_statement_changes.reason: The original phrase 'no constant C<infinity' literally includes negative constants, for which the displayed lower bound is trivially true. Requiring 0<C<infinity states the intended positive link-density lower-bound constant and is necessary for division and the contradiction argument.
